children: A project team of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party on Thursday compiled a draft proposal calling for the government to quickly establish tax measures to address soaring condominium prices.
The team falls under the LDP's Headquarters for Foreign Nationals Policy.
It is believed that the draft proposal is aimed at curbing speculative trading of condominiums by strengthening taxation on short-term capital gains, regardless of the seller's nationality.

The draft proposal also included a demand to make legislative amendments to introduce a permit system for the acquisition of land deemed critical to national security. The project team plans to submit the draft proposal to the government soon.

Regarding soaring condominium prices, the draft proposal pointed out that there is a "concern that residential real estate in urban areas is being acquired for speculative purposes." It urged the government to swiftly implement tax measures while continuing to study transactions involving foreign nationals. "Speculative transactions should be curbed regardless of whether Japanese or foreign nationals are involved," the draft said.

The Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism Ministry has compiled similar tax reform requests, so the draft proposal will likely accelerate discussions by the government and ruling parties on the matter. The main item on the agenda will likely center on raising tax rates on short-term transactions, which are viewed as a driver of price increases. According to the ministry, 12.1% of newly built condominiums purchased in Tokyo's six central wards in 2024 were resold within a year.

The draft proposal also called for the government to swiftly revise the law on reviewing and regulating real estate use surrounding important facilities and on remote islands, which currently only requires prior notification for acquiring critical land. The proposal aims to deter "individuals with malicious intent," such as those planning drone attacks on Self-Defense Forces bases.

The draft called for introducing a prior approval system for land transactions within about one kilometer of facilities vulnerable to drone attacks, as well as on uninhabited border islands, regardless of the nationality of the buyer. It also stipulated that "foreign governments or individuals who can influence the activities of foreign governments" should generally be excluded from the transactions.
